1:
Three of the commentators think the verse is in the wrong chapter. Clarke says it properly belongs to the preceding one and should on no account be separated from it, since it has the strictest connection there and none here. Robertson calls it a wrong chapter division outright, and notes that the same formula closes each of the five great discourses in this Gospel. Henry reports the same view more mildly, that some join it to the chapter before and not unfitly.

What the closing formula implies is worked out at length. Robertson takes the participle rendered commanding to mean giving orders in detail, item by item. Calvin makes the same point from the word Matthew chose, which he calls emphatic: the Twelve did not receive a commission to do as they pleased but were restricted and enjoined both as to what they should say and as to how they should conduct themselves. Henry presses it further — Christ’s commissions imply commands, so that preaching was not merely permitted to them but laid on them as a necessity — and adds that the instructions Christ gives are full instructions, since he goes through with his work. Clarke divides the two verbs that follow into the two grand parts of a minister’s duty, teaching being private instruction given to whoever came and preaching a public proclamation.

Where Jesus went, and why, produces a real disagreement. Chrysostom explains the withdrawal as deliberate: he gave the Twelve room and time to do what he had enjoined, because while he was present and healing no one would go to them instead. Robertson names that reading and rejects it. If Jesus made his own tour of the chief cities of Galilee he must have touched many of the same places, so the picture is rather of a master following behind at some distance, as he later did with the seventy; and the tour ends with the apostles gathering again at Capernaum to report. Rabanus reads the movement differently again, as Christ now fulfilling in action what he had taught in words, and offering his preaching to the Jews first. Remigius sees a descent from the particular to the general — from private teaching given to disciples to public preaching in the cities, as from heaven to earth, so that all might have light — and draws from it the lesson that preachers should study to benefit everyone. Henry has a homelier figure for the separation: the master withdrew as a nurse withdraws her hand, so that the child learns to walk alone, and it was expedient that he should go away for a while to prepare them for his long departure, so that they should not always be children.

On the geography Barnes and Ellicott differ in confidence rather than substance. Barnes places the giving of the directions in the neighbourhood of Capernaum and has Jesus go to the cities round about, in Galilee and not yet in Judea. Ellicott declines to name the spot, since Matthew does not, but argues from an earlier verse that it was probably open country rather than any city; he infers from the disciples’ return, implied later in the chapter, that the Baptist’s messengers arrived while Jesus was still working without them. On the phrase their cities he grants that the grammar might point to the towns the Twelve had visited or came from, but takes it as used loosely for the cities of Galilee at large. Clarke reads it more simply as the cities of the Jews, and Gill only notes that the departure came about in the course of things, as had been determined beforehand. Henry supplies the strategy: Christ went where he had sent the Twelve ahead of him to work miracles, so that expectation was raised and the way prepared, as John had prepared it by bringing people to repentance though he did no miracles.
2:
Why the Baptist sent at all is the largest question in the chapter, and the sources give four answers. The oldest is that he was not asking for himself. Gregory sets it out carefully: at the Jordan John had already declared this to be the Redeemer of the world, so the enquiry from prison cannot mean he doubted it; what he wants to know is whether the one who had come in person into this world would in person descend also to the world below. Jerome reads the question the same way and notices that the wording supports it — not art thou he that hast come but he that is to come — so that the sense is, tell me whether I am to announce thee to the spirits beneath. The Gloss guards the reading against a misuse, insisting that neither writer meant the unbelievers there would be converted, only that the righteous waiting in expectation would be comforted by his approach. Hilary agrees that error was impossible for a man who had proclaimed, recognised and worshipped him, and that the Spirit’s grace did not fail him in prison; the sending was to let the disciples see the works. He then reads the episode as figure: John signifies the Law, which, shut up in bonds as its own end approached, sends men to the Gospel.

Chrysostom rejects the descent reading at length and by four arguments. John was not ignorant of the death but the first to preach it, since calling him the Lamb shows the Cross; the question does not say coming to the world beneath; a forerunner to the dead is absurd, since this life is the time of grace and after death comes judgment; and if unbelievers could believe after death, nobody would perish. His own account is pastoral. Dying, John feared to leave his followers a prey to some ruinous opinion, and knew that telling them to leave him would have been taken for humility and bound them tighter; so he waited until he could send them to see the miracles, and sent only two, chosen as readiest to believe, so that his motive should not be suspected.

Ambrose offers a third answer, that John doubted not in faith but in love: he could believe this was the coming one and still not bear to think him destined to die, as Peter also said that this should not be. He adds that the two messengers may stand for the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile. Calvin dismisses two positions at once, calling it exceedingly foolish to suppose John sent partly on his own account and equally absurd to imagine him asking what message to carry to the fathers who had died. His own reading is Chrysostom’s: John saw his journey nearly done and his disciples still hesitating, and resorted to a last expedient for curing their weakness. From it he draws a rule for pastors, that they should not bind disciples to themselves but hand them to the only Teacher.

The moderns are more cautious. Barnes says the motive is not certainly known, and allows both that it was to satisfy the disciples and that John wished to establish for himself that this was the man he had baptised. Wesley states the second option flatly, not because he doubted but to confirm their faith, and Henry lays both out and hopes John’s faith did not fail, granting that where there is true faith there may still be a mixture of unbelief. Ellicott is the one who takes the question at face value, since it comes from John and the answer is sent back to him. Clarke supplies the circumstances of the arrest, Gill names the fortress and the offence that put him there, and Robertson locates it east of the Dead Sea in the tetrarch’s territory, adding that his disciples had access to him.
3:
The phrase itself is treated as a title. Barnes and Robertson both note that he that cometh was a familiar way of naming the Messiah, long foretold and everywhere expected; Robertson adds that some rabbis applied it to a forerunner of the kingdom rather than to the king. Clarke agrees that it functions as a proper name, with deliverance necessarily implied. Calvin observes that John takes the premise for granted: that a Christ would come bringing salvation was the first lesson of Jewish religion and needed no argument, so the only thing in question is whether Jesus is that promised Redeemer. He hears in the closing clause a reproach to the disciples’ sloth, that after such plain instruction they should still be looking about, and turns it into a definition: faith rests on God’s truth, does not gaze on all sides, and will not be turned to another.

On what lay behind the question, the readings again divide. Lightfoot reasons by elimination. It was not ignorance, since John had been instructed from heaven at the baptism and had borne witness repeatedly; nor was it for the disciples’ satisfaction, since they would be unworthy of such a master if they needed more than his word; so John seems to have his own imprisonment in view, having heard that miracles of every kind were being done while he lay bound. Clarke sets out three current opinions — complete ignorance, which he rules out from John’s own recorded declarations; instruction of the disciples as the end drew near; and a middle course in which John, still expecting a secular kingdom in Judea, wanted to know whether it would begin soon — then gives his own: that the length of the confinement had begun to breed doubts, and that John took the most reasonable way of ending them, by applying to Christ himself.

Ellicott presses hardest against the protective readings. There are no adequate grounds, he says, for assuming the messengers were sent only to remove their doubts; the question comes from John and the answer is sent back to John, and no difficulty in conceiving how such a doubt could arise after such a testimony can warrant doing violence to the plain meaning of the history. His explanation is deferred hope souring into something near despair, as Jeremiah once complained that God had deceived him: week after week passed without the kingdom appearing as expected, and the very wonders reported made it worse, since they proved the power and left only the conclusion that the will was lacking. So the question is one of impatience rather than doubt — art thou the coming one of whom the prophets spoke, and if so, why tarry the wheels of thy chariot? Robertson arrives at nearly the same place by a shorter road: it had once been clear enough to John, but the prison was depressing, Jesus had done nothing to get him out of it, and he longed for reassurance.

Two smaller notes attach. Clarke records that several good manuscripts and versions read not two of his disciples but by his disciples, and Robertson adopts that reading, observing that Luke has the other. Barnes points out from the parallel account that Jesus was curing many of their infirmities and evil spirits at the very time the messengers arrived, so that an answer was ready to hand. Gill notes only that this was the message they came with and the question they were to ask. Cyril of Jerusalem stands with the ancient reading of the errand, and quotes John’s words in evidence: Christ went down into the regions beneath the earth to redeem the righteous, and would one wish the living alone to enjoy his grace, most of them unholy, and not those imprisoned since Adam — Isaiah, David, Samuel, the prophets, and John himself, who by his messengers asked this very question?
4:
The reply is indirect and everyone notices it. Gill points out that Jesus makes no express declaration that he is the Messiah and that no other is to be looked for; he sends the men back with a list instead. Calvin gives two reasons for the method: it was better that the thing should speak for itself, and the indirect answer supplied Christ’s herald with a larger subject to teach from. Nor are the miracles handed over raw, since Christ shapes them with two quotations from Isaiah, so that the disciples would learn that what the prophets said of Christ’s reign was now accomplished, and would go away with an unambiguous reply. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that these are a stronger proof than any bare assertion could be, and Clarke draws a rule from it: Christ would have men judge of him and of others only by their works, which is the only safe way of judging, since a man is credited not for professing to know things but for showing his pretensions are not empty.

Ellicott raises the objection that makes the passage difficult. Apparently no fact was reported that could not already have reached the prisoner, since Matthew has by this point recorded at least one instance of each class — a blind man, a lame man, a leper, a dead child — and the raising at Nain must also have preceded this. What the Baptist needed, he concludes, was not knowledge of fresh facts but a different way of looking at the facts he had. Robertson reaches the same point from the wording: the message was symbolic, and it was for John to interpret and not for the messengers, the reminder of the prophetic texts being the whole of it. Ellicott adds that there is no Greek word answering to the again of the English, and that Luke’s note about cures worked in that same hour means the two were to report as eyewitnesses.

The items are read both plainly and figuratively. Clarke translates the first two verbs closely — the blind look upward and contemplate the heavens their Lord has made, the lame walk about, giving the crowd full proof the cure was real — then turns the whole list into an emblem of salvation, sinners being blind to the way of truth, lame in the path of righteousness, leprous with a disease that spreads, deaf to God’s word and their own conscience, and dead through the separation that iniquity makes. He also notes that the rabbis allowed sight to the blind and the raising of the dead as works the Messiah would perform. Barnes argues comparatively: prophets had worked miracles, but none so many or so weighty, and by God’s power rather than their own name.

The last clause is where the weight falls. Robertson calls it the climax of the list. Ellicott makes it the greatest of the notes of the kingdom and reads it psychologically, supposing our Lord knew that the Baptist, whose own heart was with the poor, would feel that one who united such power with such tenderness could be nobody but the expected King. Barnes finds its force in contrast, since the poor had been overlooked by Pharisees and philosophers alike and no system before this one had troubled to instruct them. Wesley calls it the greatest mercy of all. Calvin takes it as a lesson in humility deliberately supplied, since we are proud by nature and value little that comes without outward show, so that many despise the Gospel for not being embraced by persons of rank; the answer is that it was designed for the poor and despised. Gill notes that not all the works listed were done at that moment, but the messengers had authentic evidence of them.
6:
The beatitude is read by most as a gentle rebuke, and by Ellicott as evidence about the question itself. The words, he says, at once confirm that the enquiry came from the Baptist in person and show how tenderly Christ dealt with the impatience behind it: a warning was needed, but it was given in the shape of a blessing which John was still free to claim and make his own. Robertson is blunter and calls it a rebuke to John for doubting even in prison, adding that doubt is no proof of superior intellect, scholarship or piety, and that a man in the fog should not be making serious decisions. Barnes proposes a specific offence — that John may have wanted Jesus to proclaim himself publicly as the Christ rather than keep to retirement — and answers that the works gave sufficient evidence for anyone willing to look. Wesley says only that the happiness belongs to the man not offended notwithstanding all these proofs.

The word for offence gets close attention. Barnes glosses it as a stumbling-block and offers a rendering: happy is he to whom I shall not prove a stumbling-block. Clarke traces the root to hitting against or tripping over something met in the way, and locates the danger in the national expectation of a temporal deliverer, so that many might reject Christ for his mean appearance and lose the benefit of salvation. He turns this into a rule about pride — by his poverty Christ condemns the pomp of the world, and the man who will not humble himself and become poor and vile in his own eyes cannot enter the kingdom — and observes that it is generally the poor who hear the Gospel, since the rich are too busy or too gratified to attend.

Gill catalogues the offences historically rather than psychologically. The nation stumbled at Christ’s parentage and the poverty of his parents, at the manner and the supposed place of his birth, at an education that had left him unlettered and put him to a trade, at the meanness of his public appearance and the company he kept, and at the doctrines he taught. John’s own disciples, he notes, had their separate grievances: that Jesus and his followers did not fast or live the austere life theirs did, that the kingdom looked so obscure, that their master was in prison, and that reproach and persecution seemed likely to follow any profession of Christ.

Calvin generalises the saying into a warning about the whole Christian life. The clause is spoken by way of anticipation, to fortify us in advance, and the first lesson is that anyone who means to hold the faith of the Gospel must expect to contend with offences, since Christ himself is justly called a rock of offence and a stone of stumbling over which many fall. That this happens through our own fault does not excuse us; the fault is itself remedied by the blessing pronounced here, from which it follows that unbelievers have no excuse however many stumbling-blocks they plead. He then lists what actually causes the stumbling: that Christ appears with his cross, disfigured and despised; that he calls us to share his afflictions; that his glory is spiritual and therefore worthless to the world; that his doctrine runs clean against our senses; and that Satan raises disturbances calculated to make the name of Christ hateful. Men are not merely willing to withdraw, he says, but actively hunt for the means of doing so.
7:
Every commentator takes the eulogy as damage control. Chrysostom sets the problem out: enough had been done for the messengers, but the crowd had drawn wrong conclusions from the question, not knowing why John sent it. They might suppose the man who had borne such witness had changed his mind, or was jealous, or had lost his nerve in prison, or had spoken empty words all along. Christ answers for John by their own testimony rather than his own assertion: such multitudes would never have hurried into the desert unless they expected someone steadier than rock. He notes too that Christ does not expose their suspicions openly, as he did the scribes’ evil thoughts, because this came of ignorance and not malice, and adds that inconstancy is either natural or acquired by long self-indulgence, and John was neither sort. Hilary states the purpose in one line, and Ellicott the risk: those who had heard the question might think of John with undue harshness or even contempt. Henry reads it as a courtesy returned, John having testified to Christ in his retirement and Christ now testifying to John under a cloud, and draws the duty of forestalling ill thoughts of our brethren.

Why Christ waited for the messengers to leave is answered differently. Chrysostom and Henry say it was to avoid the appearance of flattery, Henry adding that praise should not be reported back in a way that might puff a man up; Wesley agrees he would probably not have said so much in their hearing. Ellicott has him turn to the crowd before they were quite out of earshot. Robertson places the eulogy as they were on their way and wonders whether it is a regret that they could not carry it back as comfort, since it proved near enough a funeral oration, Herodias compassing John’s death not long after.

The reed is read as an image and then as an argument. Barnes explains the natural history: the annual flooding of the Jordan produced great quantities of light, fragile canes easily moved by wind, an apt figure for a changeable man, and John’s sending to ask might have suggested exactly that. Robertson catalogues the word’s other uses, a staff, a measuring rod, a writer’s pen, and sums up: the reeds by the Jordan bent with the wind, but not so John. Ellicott agrees on the imagery but observes that the singular shows it was meant symbolically, of one swayed by every gust of popular feeling. Gregory says the question is put not to assert but to deny, and makes the reed a type of the carnal mind, which leans whichever way the breath of praise or detraction reaches it. Jerome dramatises the alternatives — was it a man carried about by every wind, so light-minded that he now doubts what he once preached, or one stung by envy and preaching for gain? — and answers from John’s diet of locusts and wild honey. He then allegorises: the desert is what the Spirit has deserted, and the reed is a man outwardly pious and inwardly hollow, with no marrow in his soul.

Clarke and Calvin both turn the question on the hearers. Clarke reads the whole passage as designed to convict the scribes and Pharisees of inconsistency in acknowledging John as a divinely authorised teacher while refusing the Christ he pointed to, and makes steadiness the first of John’s excellences, without which no preacher and no private Christian can be depended on. Calvin observes that John’s name was celebrated while his doctrine was slighted, and paraphrases sharply: the journey was foolish levity if you had no fixed object, and since you went to hear God’s voice from a prophet’s mouth, what he said must stay fixed in memory. Gill notes only that the messengers were returning to their master with their report.
8:
The second question is put in the same form as the first, and Gill notes the logic: since nobody went out to watch reeds bend, and nobody could have gone to see a courtier, the crowd must have gone for something else. Barnes describes the clothing precisely — the light, thin stuff worn by effeminate persons, usually fine linen and worn chiefly for ornament — and treats it as an emblem of riches, splendour and feebleness of character, against which he sets a man coarse in exterior, hardy, firm, and by that very hardness fitted to be the forerunner of a toiling and suffering Messiah. Wesley compresses the type into a phrase, an effeminate courtier accustomed to fawning and flattery, to be looked for in palaces and not in a wilderness.

Ellicott gives the clause a sharper edge by dating it. Jewish historians record that in the early years of Herod the Great a section of the scribes went over to his policy, laid aside the sombre dress of their order and appeared in the gorgeous raiment of his other courtiers; the Herodians of the Gospels were their successors in policy and probably in manner, and the reference to kings’ houses admits of no application but the palace of Antipas, in whose prison John then lay. Ellicott goes further and traces a vindictive retaliation for these very words in the gorgeous robe with which that same tetrarch afterwards arrayed Christ in mockery.

Whether the verse condemns luxury is disputed outright. Gregory says it does: let nobody suppose there is nothing sinful in rich dress, for if the pursuit of such things were blameless the Lord would not have commended John for the coarseness of his clothing, nor would Peter have checked the desire of fine clothes in women. Jerome agrees and draws a rule of life, that an austere manner and strict preaching ought to keep clear of kings’ courts and the houses of the rich; he then reads the sentence mystically, making the kings the fallen angels who are powerful in this life, so that men enervated and destroyed by luxury are plainly in their houses and possession. Clarke takes the same side and turns it on his own century: a preacher should have nothing about him savouring of effeminacy or worldly pomp, and it is a grave mistake to think the world can be won by conforming to its fashions; but except for the colour of his coat a minister can now scarcely be told from the merest worldly man, since ruffles and powder prevail everywhere, so that the church and the world have begun to shake hands while the world keeps its enmity. He asks whether a worldly-minded preacher is not in the most peculiar sense an abomination, and adds that a preacher who dresses like the world is never in his element except at the tables of the rich.

Calvin denies the whole reading. Those who think Christ here condemns the extravagance of a court are mistaken, he says, and he grants freely that many other passages do censure luxury of dress and excessive attention to appearance. This one means only that there was nothing in the wilderness to draw people from every quarter, everything there being rude and unpolished and fit rather to inspire disgust, and that elegance which delights the eye is to be looked for in the courts of kings. Augustine had proposed a measure that cuts between the two: in such things it is not the use of the goods that is blamed but the lust of those using them, so that a man who uses what is within his reach more sparingly than those he lives among is either temperate or superstitious, while one who exceeds the practice of the good around him either has some purpose in it or is simply dissolute.
9:
The third question is the one that is answered rather than denied. Ellicott notes that it throws the hearers back on their first impressions: they had gone out to see a prophet and were not disappointed, and nothing they had heard since should make them think less of him. Barnes agrees that their estimate had been correct and then explains the comparative. Those had been reckoned greatest among the prophets who foretold the Messiah most clearly, and Isaiah stood first for the sublimity of his writing and the clearness of his prediction; but John lived in the time of the Christ, foretold his coming more clearly still, and was the instrument of introducing him to the nation, so that he stands first among the prophets. Clarke calls this a fourth excellency and adds the detail that gives it force: John not only pointed Christ out, but saw him, and had the honour of dying for the truth he had proclaimed. Robertson parses the comparative as an ablative and notes that the word itself means exceeding, overflowing; John had every quality of a true prophet — moral conviction, integrity, strength of will, fearless zeal — and was besides the forerunner. Wesley states the difference in a line: the prophets pointed him out from far off, while John was the immediate forerunner. Gill asks the question back at the crowd, since it was neither anything so mean as a shaking reed nor anything so grand as a man in gay clothing.

The quotation that follows is examined for its wording. Ellicott observes that the Greek is not taken from the Septuagint but is a free rendering of the Hebrew, and that the change matters: in Malachi it is the Lord who speaks of his own coming and says the messenger shall prepare the way before me, while here the Lord speaks to the Christ and says before thee. Since the same prophecy had been applied to John’s work from the first in the song of Zacharias, our Lord’s adoption of it stamps the whole chapter as Messianic. Barnes locates the passage in Malachi, notes that its substance appears in Isaiah too, and reads the preparing as the fitting of the people by proper instruction. Clarke counts this the fifth excellency and suggests it was probably through this preaching that so many attached themselves to Christ as soon as he appeared. Gill and Wesley do no more than mark the citation.

The older readings press the word messenger. Gregory explains that the Greek word means one sent with a message, and argues from it that John is more than a prophet by office as well as by timing: a prophet’s business is to foretell what is coming, not to show it present, whereas John pointed out as present the one he had foretold by going before him. Jerome makes the same point about the title and guards it — John is called an angel not as sharing the angelic nature but from the dignity of his office as forerunner — and adds that his prophetic privilege carried with it the further honour of baptising his Lord. Pseudo-Chrysostom marks the difference from all the rest: the other prophets were sent to announce Christ’s coming, but John to prepare his way. He also settles a small point of time, that the crowds had not gone out into the desert on this occasion, since John was by then in prison; the question looks back to the days when he was still in the wilderness and the people flocked to him. The Gloss defines the preparing narrowly, as the opening of the hearers’ hearts by preaching repentance and baptising.
11:
The first half of the verse is read as a bounded superlative. Jerome insists on the limits: John is set before those born in wedlock and not before the one born of a virgin, and the words make him only equal to the patriarchs and prophets, since it does not follow that because none are greater than he, he is greater than all. He adds that any saint already with the Lord is greater than one still in the field, a crown being one thing and a battle another. Pseudo-Chrysostom reasons the opposite way: the saints rank in a fixed order under divine judgment, so he who has none greater than himself is greater than all. Raban and Cyril of Jerusalem fasten on the same word, women and not virgins, Raban explaining the translator’s usage and Cyril making the comparison one among fellow-servants, so that Elijah, Enoch and Moses are none of them greater while the Son lies beyond comparison with servants. Chrysostom notes that Christ added his own verdict to the prophet’s and had to guard it at once, lest the praise tempt the Jews to set John above him. Gill observes how solemnly the claim is made.

Who the lesser person is has been contested since antiquity. Augustine reports that heretics used the verse to deny that John, still less the earlier prophets, belonged to the kingdom, and offers two constructions in reply. Either the kingdom is what has not yet been received, whose members are angels, so the least of them exceeds a righteous man with a corruptible body; or it is the church of all the righteous, and the Lord speaks of himself, later than John in birth but greater in divine nature, which requires repunctuating the sentence to read that he who is less than John is in the kingdom greater than he. Chrysostom mentions in passing that some referred the words to the apostles.

Ellicott and Calvin both reject the self-referring reading outright. Ellicott calls it strange that so many have taken it so, and gives two reasons: it would be a poor truism to announce that the King outranks his herald, and Christ nowhere else speaks of himself in such terms. Calvin calls the same view a strange blunder, since nothing here concerns personal rank and the whole commendation falls on pre-eminence of office — a point he says Luke’s wording makes plain by restricting the eminence to teaching. Ellicott then takes the comparative strictly and identifies the little ones who believe, whose knowledge of the truth exceeds John’s though their fame and austerity fall below it; Calvin sets the ministers of the Gospel above John as John stood above the prophets, since he proclaimed redemption at hand where they spoke of it at a distance and under shadows.

The moderns divide over how far down the comparison reaches. Barnes doubts it can be said of the obscurest Christian that his views are clearer than Isaiah’s, and restricts it to the apostles who heard Christ’s own instruction. Clarke insists instead on the meanest preacher of a risen Saviour, with three cautions: the kingdom here is not future glory, the superiority is not in holiness, and it lies merely in the difference of ministry, since John did not live to see the Spirit poured out. He quotes a rabbinic saying that the servant maid who passed through the Red Sea saw what Ezekiel never saw. Wesley cites an older writer that one perfect in the law is inferior to one baptised into Christ’s death, John having been cut off before the kingdom was given. Robertson settles the paradox in a phrase: John is greater than all in character, and the least in the kingdom surpasses him in privilege, because John is the mountain peak between the old and the new and all who come after stand on his shoulders.
12:
The verb is the difficulty. Ellicott notes that it can be middle, meaning that the kingdom forces its way, or passive, as the English has it, and judges the passive right with little doubt; the noun that follows is without the article, so the sense is men who are violent, and the picture is a city attacked on every side by people eager to possess it. There is no thought of hostility in the words: the violent are men of impetuous zeal, snatching peace and pardon as men carry off the spoil of a captured town. Robertson keeps the question open: the verb occurs only here and once in Luke, the papyri show both uses, and either voice makes sense though a different sense — passively the kingdom is stormed like a conquered city, in the middle it forces its own way like a rushing wind. What the saying records at least is an impetuous thronging around Jesus that John’s preaching had set off.

Whether the verse describes a historical rush or a rule for the individual soul is where the disagreement bites. Barnes takes it as a statement of fact: a great crowd pressed to hear John and the same had continued, the image being of besiegers at walls. He then denies the other reading outright — there is no allusion here, he says, to the manner in which individual sinners seek salvation. Clarke asserts exactly that reading. The tax-gatherers and heathens whom the scribes thought had no right to the kingdom seized the offered mercy and took it from the doctors who claimed its chief places; and whoever will possess that kingdom of righteousness and peace must be in earnest, since all hell will oppose him at every step, and a man not absolutely determined will perish. Calvin stands with Clarke on the substance while adding a restriction Clarke does not. Christ speaks honourably of the Gospel because the Spirit put such efficacy into one man’s doctrine that it kindled zeal in crowds, which shows it came from God; but the second clause limits the violence to men of one class, since most were no more moved than if John had been acting a play that had nothing to do with them. Those who pass the power of God by are therefore inexcusable, and the verse shows what faith is: not cold assent but warm affection rushing forward as in a struggle. Lightfoot reads the whole clause as further praise of John, since the sheer numbers and zeal of those who crowded in argue the worth of the teacher and his doctrine.

The older readings identify the violent differently. Gregory has sinners defiled with evil deeds return in penitence and enter, as sinners, into another’s place, taking the heavenly throne by violence. Jerome locates the violence in the disparity itself: it is a great violence that men born of earth should seek a dwelling in heaven and obtain by excellence what they do not have by nature. Hilary reads it nationally: the apostles were sent to the lost sheep of Israel, but the profit of their preaching went to publicans and sinners, so the glory owed to the fathers and offered by Christ is entered and held by force through the might of the Gentiles. Chrysostom keeps it simple — all who come in haste take the kingdom through faith — and notes the argumentative use, that if all things were fulfilled until John, then Jesus is the one who should come. The Gloss states the purpose of the sentence: it is added lest the previous verse leave anyone supposing John a stranger to the kingdom. Gill and Wesley mark the span of time, Wesley adding the image of men taking a city by storm.
13:
The verse is taken as the boundary line of two dispensations. Barnes states it plainly: John introduced a new one, and the old, in which the prophets and the law of Moses were the guide, closed when he began to preach that the kingdom was at hand; by the law he understands the five books of Moses and by the prophets the rest of the Old Testament. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that in John the old dispensation expired and the new began. Ellicott notices that the usual order of the two words is inverted, the prophets coming first because the stress falls on the prophetic rather than the legislative side of the earlier revelation: their work pointed to a kingdom in the far-off latter days, while John saw it close at hand and announced that it had actually appeared.

Gill argues the same point as a further proof of John’s superiority. The writers before him spoke of a Messiah still to come, and spoke either in obscure terms or under dark shadows and figures, whereas John spoke of him as already arrived, in plain words, and pointed to his very person. He then presses further than the others: since John there have been no prophecies of the Messiah and his kingdom at all, vision and prophecy being now sealed up, which he says the Jews themselves acknowledge in the saying that the prophets prophesied only of the days of the Messiah. Jerome had guarded against exactly that inference. The verse does not cut off all prophets after John, he says, since the Acts records that Agabus prophesied and that Philip had four daughters who did so too; the meaning is only that the written Law and Prophets, whatever else they spoke of, prophesied of the Lord.

Clarke takes a different route through the verb. He believes the word here means that they taught, or continued to instruct, so that the prophets are the instructors of the people concerning a Christ who was to come, and their office ends when John shows that all their predictions and all the types and ceremonies are now about to be fully and finally accomplished, Christ being at last revealed. Calvin also calls the word emphatic, but draws from it a contrast rather than a definition: the law did not set God before men’s eyes, but represented him under figures and shadows as one absent, and the comparison is meant to show how criminal it is to stay indifferent once the presence of God has been manifested to those whom prediction had held so long in suspense. He is careful, though, not to promote John too far. Christ does not here class him with the ministers of the Gospel, having already given him a station between them and the prophets, and there is no inconsistency in that: John’s preaching was indeed a part of the Gospel, but it was little more than a first lesson.
14:
The conditional clause is read by everyone as a warning of resistance. Gill hears in it a suspicion of unbelief and hardness, as though they would not receive it, and adds that whether they would or not the thing was true. Lightfoot says the words hint the same suspicion, and observes that the obstinate expectation of the nation down to his own day, that Elijah is still to come in person, bears it out; on what ground some Christians hold the same opinion, he adds drily, let them look to it. Barnes explains the form of speech as marking a doctrine different from the common view, which his hearers might therefore be disposed to reject: they looked for Elijah to appear in person, and for Jeremiah and other prophets besides, to grace the Messiah’s advent. Ellicott agrees that our Lord was consciously setting aside a popular and strongly fixed belief, and puts the sense as an offer — if you are willing and able to receive that John was in very deed doing Elijah’s work, you need look for no other. Calvin turns the exception into a charge, glancing at a hardened obstinacy that shuts its eyes against the clearest light, while insisting that John’s commission does not depend on their approval; the fault charged is carelessness and ingratitude in withholding the respect he is owed.

How John can be Elijah is answered the same way by all who address it, and guarded carefully. Barnes says the prophecy evidently meant not that Elijah should appear in person but that one should appear closely resembling him, as Luke has it, in the spirit and power of Elijah. Ellicott notes how durable the literal expectation has been, a vacant chair still set for Elijah at great solemnities and even Christian interpreters expecting him in person before the second Advent, and takes the angel’s words to Zacharias as the true sense, here confirmed. Remigius states the distinction in a line: Christ did not say John was Elijah in person, but in the Spirit. Chrysostom notes that the conditional form shows their freedom and asks a willing mind of them, and then puts the identity as a reciprocal one — John is Elijah and Elijah is John, because both were forerunners of Christ. Jerome sets a firmer boundary. John is called Elijah not in the manner of the foolish philosophers and certain heretics who bring forward the passing of the soul from one body into another, but because he came in the spirit and power of Elijah with the same measure of the Spirit; and Jerome then draws the resemblance out in detail, the austerity of life and fortitude of spirit, the desert, the girdle of skins, and the pair of denunciations that cost each man dear — Elijah forced to flee for reproving Ahab and Jezebel, John beheaded for condemning the union of Herod and Herodias. Robertson observes that Jesus endorses John as Malachi’s promise even though John had himself denied being Elijah, and that Christ emphasises the point with the words that follow. Clarke works from the prediction instead, extracting three marks from Malachi — that the messenger should be the Messiah’s forerunner, that he should appear before the destruction of the second temple, and that he should preach repentance before the land was smitten with a curse — and argues that all three fit John and nobody else, which he takes as proof that Jesus was the promised Christ. He also asks that the name be spelled as in the Old Testament, so that the two agree. Wesley simply marks the citation from Malachi.
15: The formula that closes the passage is agreed on all hands to mark difficulty. Barnes and Wesley both call it proverbial and take it as a demand for the highest attention; Barnes adds that the doctrine about John was of the greatest importance, and that whoever can understand or believe that this is the promised Elijah should remember it. Ellicott notes that it appears here for the first time and that Christ seems to have used it habitually after teaching, parabolic or otherwise, that needed more than ordinary thought — taking in this new aspect of Elijah’s coming required the insight men needed to read the parable of the Sower without an interpreter. Calvin makes the same observation about the formula and adds a reason for the deafness: many hearers have their ears closed, and since every man is hindered not only by his own unbelief but by the influence men have on one another, Christ exhorts those whose ears have been pierced to weigh the secret attentively rather than stay deaf with the rest. Gill takes the same view of its use, that Christ employs it when something serious and not easily understood has been delivered and attention is required; and he lists what has just been said — that John was more than a prophet and more excellent than all the prophets, that the law and the prophets were now at an end, and that John was Elijah — as things which, rightly understood, would have settled the hearers’ judgment about Christ himself. His conclusion is that not everyone had the spiritual hearing to take in matters of that height, and that those who did should weigh them seriously; he adds that the phrase is met with in Jewish writings. Clarke turns it into a complaint instead. The things said are so clear and manifest, he argues, that a man need only hear them to be convinced and fully satisfied of their truth; and since neither that generation nor those after it have heard or considered them, but stop their ears at the subject, they show not merely a bad cause but a ruined one, being willingly blind and refusing to come to the light.
16:
The picture is agreed on. Barnes and Ellicott both describe children imitating what they have seen adults do, getting up a wedding with pipes and dancing and a funeral with wailing, then quarrelling because the others will not join. Robertson traces the marketplace from assembly to public square, where people gathered to trade or talk, notes that eastern bazaars are now held in streets rather than squares, and remarks that children play in streets still. Henry observes that the whole thing was a jest and so made no impression, which is his point of comparison, notes that Christ pauses as though at a loss for a similitude, and calls it the greatest absurdity to have good preaching and be none the better for it. Clarke translates the second complaint closely: the verb means to beat the breast in lamentation, and there is an allusion to the funeral wailing described earlier in the Gospel.

Who is playing which part is genuinely disputed. Barnes gives the common reading: one group is sullen and will not join, the others complain that they have tried both games in vain — John came abstaining and displeased them, the Son of man came living like other men and displeased them equally. Wesley puts the same reading in a line, that this generation resembles the froward children of whom their playfellows complain. Ellicott reverses it. He identifies the children who issue the invitation with the generation Christ condemns, so that it is they who were loud against John for refusing their self-indulgent mirth and bitter against Jesus for refusing their hypocritical austerity. He grants the commoner explanation an adequate sense but denies it fits the wording, and rests the point on a reading of the text — not their fellows but the others. Clarke supplies the same variant, noting that many of the best manuscripts carry it and that the two words are so alike the confusion is easily explained.

The older commentators identify the children differently again. Hilary makes them the prophets, who preached in singleness of meaning and reprove the people in the midst of the synagogue — his rendering of the marketplace — for not following their words as dancers follow the measure; the prophets had called them to confess in song, as Moses, Isaiah and David did. Jerome takes them for the children of the prophet’s saying, Behold I and the children whom the Lord has given me, and has them put the dilemma directly: if fasting pleased you, why not John, and if fullness, why not the Son of man? Remigius raises the obvious objection to any such reading, asking whether unbelieving Jews could really be called fellows of the prophets, and answers that they are so called only because they sprang from one stock. The Gloss takes the generation to include Christ and John along with the Jews, so that the sense is: John is thus great, yet you would believe neither him nor me.

Chrysostom states the strategy behind the two ministries. Nothing had been omitted for their salvation: an unrestricted life was shown them and did not convince, a hard life was lived before them and was not heeded, and the two say the same thing, having one object. He likens the two to hunters driving the same quarry from opposite sides, and explains why the severity fell to John: men admire fasting, so John was reared to it from infancy that his words might carry weight, and it counted for more that such a man should bear witness to Christ than that Christ should live so himself. Christ besides had the witness of miracles, which John had not. Gill reduces the whole to its result, that they were pleased with nothing and with no man’s ministry, but found fault with whatever they heard or saw done.
17:
The two complaints are the two halves of the children’s game, and the commentators fill in what the game imitated. Gill explains that Jewish children, having watched their parents and friends at festivals and weddings where some played the pipe and others danced, mimicked the same in their own diversions, and having watched the mourning women at funerals making their doleful ditties while others answered them, acted those parts too, expecting their playfellows to take the responses and finding that they would not. Clarke reads the first line the same way — the music was begun and should have been followed by the dance, and was not — and translates the second closely: the verb means to strike or beat the breast, particularly in lamentation, a usage he finds in the best Greek and Roman writers as well as in the prophets and elsewhere in the Gospels, and there is an allusion to the funeral wailing described earlier in this Gospel.

Robertson lingers over the scene itself. The same parable appears in Luke, and he asks whether Jesus had played such games as a child in Nazareth, remarking that he had certainly watched them often since and that his interest in children was keen enough to have created the modern child’s world out of the indifference of the past. The children in the picture, he adds, would not play either wedding or funeral, and did it in a peevish fret; these metaphors are vivid to anyone with eyes to see. He gives the same rendering as Clarke for the mourning, a direct middle meaning to beat the heart after the fashion of eastern funeral lamentation.

Origen takes the mention of dancing somewhere else entirely. He recalls how John, filled with a divine spirit and neither cowed by royal dignity nor silenced by fear of death, told Herod plainly that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife; and how Herod, not daring to kill him outright and take the prophetic word from the people, bound him and put him in prison. Then the dancing of another man’s daughter, whose movements seemed harmonious and pleased a king fond of birthday celebrations, became the cause that there was no longer a prophetic head among that people. Origen presses the figure onto the nation: the movements of the Jewish people, which seem to be according to the law, were nothing else than the movements of that daughter, and her dancing stands opposed to the holy dancing which those who have not danced will be reproached for missing.
18:
The verse begins the explanation of the parable, and the first thing settled is what the description means. Gill insists that neither eating nor drinking cannot be taken absolutely, since John could not otherwise have lived to discharge his office. He ate sparingly and very little; what he ate was not the common food of men, for he took neither bread nor wine but locusts and wild honey; and he excused every invitation to a house, shunning all feasts and entertainments and all sociable eating and drinking. Gill adds the sting: the scribes and Pharisees made great professions of abstinence and frequent fasting, yet had no wish to follow so severe a way of living, and instead of lamenting in answer to his mournful ditty they answered with a slander.

Augustine reaches the same reading of the phrase by another road and puts it to work as an argument. He challenges the Manichaeans to say what Christ ate and drank, given that he here describes himself as eating and drinking by comparison with a man who did neither. John did not in fact drink nothing at all, but drank no wine or strong drink, only water; nor did he go without food altogether, but ate only locusts and wild honey. Whence, then, is he said to have come neither eating nor drinking, except that he did not use the food the Jews used? And unless the Lord had used that food, he could not have been called, in comparison with John, one who came eating and drinking. It would be strange indeed, Augustine observes, if the man who ate locusts and honey were said to come neither eating nor drinking while the man who ate only bread and herbs were said to come eating and drinking.

On the accusation the readers agree about its form and differ only in emphasis. Ellicott notes that the phrase was a common one, asserting at once the fact of insanity and assigning demoniacal possession as its cause, and that this was the explanation the scribes gave of John’s austerities: to them the locusts and wild honey were simply the diet of a madman. Wesley glosses it the same way, as a charge of melancholy under the influence of an evil spirit, and marks the resemblance of the austere manner to Elijah’s. Clarke reads the charge as a symptom rather than a judgment, and draws two maxims from it. A sinner will not be persuaded that anything he has no mind to imitate can come from God; and there are men who would rather blame holiness itself than esteem it in people they dislike. The accusation itself he paraphrases bluntly, that John was called a vile hypocrite driven by a demon to deceive and destroy the simple.
19:
Gill sets the second half of the comparison against the first: Christ ate and drank as men usually do, was free and sociable, went to feasts and weddings when invited, and was affable and friendly to everyone. Clarke asks how one could fast rigidly who had no corrupt appetite to mortify, and draws the conclusion for everyone else: whatever course the followers of God take they will not escape the world’s censure, and the best way is not to be concerned at it, since iniquity in contradicting the divine conduct often ends by exposing itself. Ellicott points the phrasing at the feast in Matthew’s house and the marriage at Cana, and hears in it the earlier complaint about eating with publicans and sinners. Robertson holds both charges exaggerations, since John had no demon and Jesus was neither glutton nor winebibber, and finds the third title worst: the word for friend carries a sinister force, implying Jesus was the comrade of the worst characters and like them in conduct. It began as a malicious nickname, he says, and is now a name of honour.

The closing sentence is disputed in its text. Jerome reports that some copies read justified of her works instead of her children, and prefers that, on the ground that wisdom does not seek the witness of words but of works. Clarke records the same variant with its manuscript and versional support. Robertson observes the opposite pressure, that some manuscripts import the wording of the parallel in Luke, and renders the verb as a timeless aorist meaning to be set right.

What the children are is disputed too. Clarke lays out three constructions: that Christ applies the title Wisdom to himself, as he has just applied Son of man, with the description in Proverbs behind it; that the children are John and himself, teachers commending wisdom by pure doctrine and holy living; or that children stands by a Hebrew idiom for the fruits of a thing, as sparks are called the children of the coal, which he thinks led some witnesses to read works. Jerome makes the children the apostles, who prove the doctrine of God, or Christ himself who is the power and wisdom of God, to have acted righteously. Augustine adds what those apostles understood: that the kingdom of God lies not in meat and drink but in patient endurance, so abundance does not lift such men up nor want cast them down. Hilary assigns the justifying to those who seize the kingdom by faith, confessing wisdom just in transferring its gift from the rebellious, and argues that Christ is wisdom by nature and not by his deeds, against those who evade the apostle’s statement by saying only that wisdom and power were shown mightily in his birth of a virgin — a power and its effect not being the same thing.

On what the vindication amounts to the readings differ in temper. Chrysostom makes it an acquittal rather than a persuasion: though nothing was effected by the goodness extended to them, he fulfils his own part and leaves them nothing to accuse him of. Robertson finds the plan of God justified by its results, since that wisdom deliberately arranged two unlike lives and does not require everyone to be alike in everything; the generation, he says, is childish rather than childlike, full of whimsical inconsistencies in its faultfinding. Ellicott presses the tense as a generalised fact and stretches the saying across the ages: the evil world rejects everyone who tries to overcome its evil, each on some pretext, but a true seeker after wisdom welcomes holiness in whatever form it appears, cheerful or ascetic, so long as it is real. Wesley reduces it to a sentence, that this wisdom is acknowledged by those who are truly wise.
20:
The Gloss marks the turn: up to this point the accusation had been brought against the Jews in general, and now it is directed at particular towns by name, places where Christ had specially preached and which still would not be converted. Jerome states the ground of the reproach in one sentence — that after so many wonders had been done among them they had not repented — and observes that the word used is one of mourning, so that these Galilean towns are lamented rather than merely denounced. Gill fills in the occasion. Christ had sent out his disciples and had himself taught and preached in these cities, confirming his doctrine with many wonderful works; he had watched how they treated both John and himself, calling the one possessed and the other a licentious man; and finding that they could be pleased with neither ministry he seasonably and righteously reproached them for their ingratitude, their unbelief and the hardness of their hearts. Barnes glosses the verb plainly as reproving, rebuking, or denouncing heavy judgment.

Wesley notices something the others pass over: it is observable that Christ had never upbraided these cities before, and that at first they had received him with all gladness, Capernaum in particular. Clarke turns the fact into a principle, that the more God has done to draw men to himself the less excusable they are if they continue in iniquity; and he adds the converse, that if Christ had not done everything necessary for their salvation he could not have reproached them for their impenitence.

Calvin follows Luke for the date and the motive. The words were spoken while Christ was sending the disciples into various parts of the country to announce that the kingdom of God was at hand, and they arose from his reflecting on the ingratitude of a people among whom he had long discharged a prophet’s office and worked many wonders to no result. They announce, in effect, that the time had come for him to depart to other cities, having learned by experience that the inhabitants around that lake were full of obstinacy and desperate malice. Calvin then draws attention to what is absent: nothing is said here about the doctrine, and the reproach is simply that the miracles had not led them to repent. The purpose of such displays of power was to invite men to Christ, but since all are by nature averse to him the invitation must begin with repentance. Ellicott raises the question of arrangement rather than motive. The same rebuke appears in Luke inside the charge to the Seventy, and he refuses to conclude that Matthew has compiled a discourse out of separately collected fragments; it is far more natural to believe that our Lord used the same or nearly the same forms of speech on different occasions.

Robertson works on the phrase for the works themselves. The Greek may be elative, as such forms usually are in the papyri, giving his very many mighty works, though the ordinary superlative also makes sense here. He then sets out the vocabulary of miracle across the New Testament: this word carries the notion of power, another means a wonder or portent and occurs only in the plural and always paired with the word for sign, a third means work and is common in John, and there are others besides meaning strange, glorious and wonderful.
21:
Wesley and Clarke both object to the English. These are not curses, Wesley says, but a compassionate declaration of the misery the cities were bringing on themselves; Clarke would render the exclamation alas for thee rather than woe to thee, the first being pity and the second a denunciation of wrath, and holds Christ meant the first. Jerome had said as much, that the word is one by which these towns are mourned for.

The places themselves are difficult. Robertson notes that Chorazin is named only here and in the parallel, proof both of how meagre our knowledge of that Judaism is and of how much the Gospels leave untold. Ellicott finds it more striking that no miracle is recorded at either town, and turns the silence into an argument for the genuineness of the words: they were no afterthought dovetailed into the narrative, nor was the narrative expanded to explain them. Jerome had faced the same question and answered from the summary that Christ went about the towns and villages healing every sickness, among which these two may be supposed to fall. Barnes and Clarke both make Bethsaida the home of Philip, Andrew and Peter, Clarke adding that one impenitent town furnished three of the Twelve. Chrysostom makes the fact an aggravation: Bethsaida is named so that nobody should call these people evil by nature, and it proves extreme wickedness that they were worse not only than any then living but than the worst of past time. Raban reads the names as meanings — Chorazin as my mystery, Bethsaida as the house of fruits or of hunters — so that Christ mourns towns which once had the mystery of God, ought to have borne the fruit of virtues, and had spiritual hunters sent into them; and these towns would not believe when the Lord came in person, while Tyre and Sidon believed later at the apostles’ preaching.

The comparison with the heathen cities is the sting. Lightfoot puts it starkly: cities of a cursed seed and name, had they seen these miracles, would not have hardened into such madness but would have turned from their heathenism, or at least reached a repentance sufficient to avert vengeance, as Nineveh did without being saved by it. Calvin explains the rhetorical purpose: no Jew looked on those places as anything but abominable despisers of God, so the curse is heightened by saying there would have been more hope of reformation where there was no religion at all. He then warns against thorny questions about secret decrees: the discourse is accommodated to ordinary human capacity, and reasons not from what God foresaw but from what both parties would have done so far as the facts allow judging. The corruption of Tyre and Sidon might be laid to ignorance, no voice of God having been heard there; the obstinacy of the Galilean towns could not. Ellicott takes the words further than Calvin will allow, finding in them the ultimate law of God’s dealings with the heathen: men are judged not only by what they have done but by what they would have done under other conditions, that is, according to their opportunities. Clarke reads long ago as pointing back to Ezekiel’s denunciations, so the sense is what those cities would have done had a prophet worked such miracles among them; he explains the sackcloth from a religious mendicant’s coarse cloth sprinkled with ashes. Gregory gives the sign a meaning: the roughness of sackcloth is conscience pricked and the ashes are the dust of the dead, the one reminding us of our sins and the other of what judgment has made us. Gill reports a conjecture that the name, meaning wooded places, covered Cana and a small wooded district. Robertson observes that this verse and the next both assume a condition known to be unfulfilled, and that neither city changed its conduct.
22:
Gill insists on the certainty of what follows. It may be depended on as true and will certainly come to pass, however the inhabitants of these cities flattered themselves, and in whatever light they had been used to view their Phoenician neighbours — fancying themselves the favourites of heaven and those others the most execrable of creatures. Lightfoot supplies the idiom: both this phrase and its longer form, the day of the great judgment, were ordinary Jewish speech, so that Christ is using a formula his hearers knew well and turning it against them. The comparison itself is the point, since the two names were bywords for a heathenism the nation held in contempt, and the sentence sets them on the better side of the ledger.

Clarke draws the principle out of the comparison. Everything will help to overwhelm the impenitent at the tribunal of God — not only the sins they have committed but the benefits and favours they have received, so that privilege itself appears on the other side of the account. Wesley marks the difference between the general threat and this particular one: beyond the denunciation of woe pronounced on stubborn unbelievers, the degree of their misery will be greater than that of Tyre and Sidon, and greater even than Sodom’s. The threat is therefore not merely repeated but raised, and raised by a measure the hearers themselves would have supplied.

Remigius takes two things from the form of the sentence. Because the words say it shall be easier for one place than for another in the day of judgment, they prove that there are different punishments in hell just as there are different mansions in the kingdom of heaven; the comparative would be meaningless if the penalty were uniform. He also notes a point of usage that governs this whole passage: when the Lord speaks of a city or a country he is not chiding the buildings and the walls but the people who live there, the thing containing being put for the thing contained. It is a small observation, but it turns what sounds like a curse on stone into a sentence on men.
23:
Gill notes that this city is singled out from all the rest and addressed on its own because of its peculiar advantages, and the readers divide over what those advantages were. Barnes takes the exaltation broadly: the city was prosperous, successful in commerce and favoured in wealth, and most of all favoured by the presence, the preaching and the miracles of Christ, who spent much of the early part of his ministry there. Ellicott restricts it deliberately. He lists the wonders recorded at Capernaum — the nobleman’s son, the demoniac, the man sick of the palsy, the mother of Peter’s wife and the many works that followed, the woman with the issue of blood, the daughter of Jairus, the centurion’s servant — besides the unrecorded signs implied elsewhere, and says that in this sense, and in no outward prosperity, had Capernaum been exalted to heaven. Wesley agrees in a line, that the honour was Christ’s presence and miracles.

On the fall the three agree in substance and differ in the word. Barnes denies that the sentence means the people should all go to hell, and reads it of a city losing its prosperity and taking the lowest place among cities, the term being set against heaven and denoting desolation rather than a place of punishment — though he grants that Christ did also threaten future punishment on those who rejected him. Clarke derives the Greek word from a root meaning unseen, treats it as the equivalent of the Hebrew term, and complains that the English rendering now misleads, since it is used only of the place of the damned; he adds that the English word itself descends from a verb meaning to cover, which is why roofing is still called heling in Cornwall and book covers go by the same name in Lancashire, so that it once expressed the original well enough. Ellicott settles it briefly: the word here means Hades, the grave, and not Gehenna, though the following verse shows the ultimate abasement of the city is also in view. All three treat the ruin as accomplished. Barnes and Clarke both observe that in the wars between the Jews and the Romans these towns were so obliterated that their former sites can hardly be determined, and Ellicott that a few conjecturally identified ruins mark Capernaum while in Chorazin and Bethsaida not one stone is left upon another.

Jerome reports that other copies make the clause a statement rather than a question, and offers two constructions of it. Either the city goes down to hell because it proudly resisted the preaching; or, having been exalted to heaven by entertaining Christ and having his mighty works done in it, it is visited with the heavier punishment for still refusing to believe them. He adds that the name means the most fair town, and finds Jerusalem condemned in it, as the prophet said that Sodom was justified by her. Calvin dwells on the honour rather than the name. It was an inestimable thing that the Son of God, beginning his reign and priesthood, chose this place for the seat of his palace and sanctuary, and resided there so constantly that many supposed it his birthplace; and it was as deeply sunk in its filth as if no drop of divine grace had ever fallen on it. From this he draws the rule that the punishment will be dreadful in proportion to the favours received, since profaning the gifts of God is sacrilege and never passes unpunished, the more eminent a man is the more severely he is punished for polluting what God gave him, and an awful vengeance awaits those who treat Christ and his Gospel with contempt after receiving his spiritual gifts.
24:
Gill takes the repeated formula as addressed to Capernaum and its inhabitants exactly as the earlier one was addressed to Chorazin and Bethsaida, and Wesley repeats his measure of the sentence, that beyond the general denunciation the degree of misery will exceed that of Tyre and Sidon and even of Sodom. Clarke reads the phrase as naming the ancient inhabitants of the city and its neighbourhood, and does the arithmetic that follows from it. Those people are said elsewhere to be suffering the vengeance of eternal fire; their destruction fell nearly nineteen centuries before the incarnation; and it is a terrible thought that it will be more tolerable for sinners already condemned some four thousand years than for men who live and die unbelieving under the Gospel. He infers degrees of punishment answering to degrees of guilt, and puts the contempt of a preached Gospel at the top of the scale. He also distinguishes two senses of the day of judgment: Sodom’s was the day it was destroyed by fire from heaven, and these towns had theirs when the Romans destroyed them, but there remains a final day beyond both.

Why the miracles were withheld from cities said to be readier to repent is the difficulty the whole passage leaves, and the sources take four positions. Jerome raises it as the point at which a careful reader must hesitate: if Tyre and Sidon would have repented at such preaching, then their unbelief is not their fault, and the sin lies with whoever declined to preach to them. His answer is short — that we do not know God’s judgments and are ignorant of the secrets of his particular dispensations.

Augustine works at it much harder. He denies that the Gospel went unpreached in the times and places where God foreknew men would be such as would not believe even at a raising of the dead. He then presses the logic of the verse itself: if the dead were judged by the deeds they would have done had they lived, these cities ought not to be punished at all, whereas the sentence says plainly that they will be punished, only less severely than the others. He reports a solution offered by a Catholic disputant of some note — that the Lord foreknew Tyre and Sidon would fall away after believing the miracles, and in mercy withheld the miracles, since to lapse from a faith once held incurs a heavier penalty than never to have held it. His own answer is the predestination of the saints, by which he means the foreknowing and making ready of the mercies through which all who are saved are certainly saved, the rest being left to a just judgment; and he allows that some men have by nature a gift of understanding that would move them to faith if they heard the words.

Remigius reaches a similar place from the other end. There were many in Chorazin and Bethsaida who would believe and many in Tyre and Sidon who would not, and were therefore not worthy of the Gospel; so the Lord preached where those who were to believe might be enabled to, and did not preach where contempt of the Gospel would only have made the unbelieving worse and their punishment heavier. He also fastens on a single word in the preceding verse, that one who knows all things says the city would perhaps have remained, and takes the deliberate uncertainty as a sign that freedom of choice is left to men. Calvin refuses the whole enquiry. Christ speaks after the manner of men and does not bring the secret purpose of God out of its sanctuary; and for quarrelsome persons one consideration removes every objection, that although God had in his own power a remedy for saving those cities, in destroying them he was a just avenger and remains righteous in his punishment.
25:
The opening verb is an idiom: Gill calls it a Hebrew way of speaking used where nothing precedes that the words could answer, and Wesley says it often means no more than speaking with reference to something before. Ellicott notes that Luke attaches the words to the return of the Seventy while Matthew, omitting that mission, must mean the Twelve. Robertson calls the utterance prayer, praise and self-communing at once. He also meets a critical difficulty: the passage is so Johannine in language that critics are disturbed to find it in an early source, the only satisfying explanation being that Jesus did speak in the strain the Fourth Gospel preserves.

What the first word means is settled the same way by several. Augustine points out that confession is not for sinners only, since one may confess by praising as well as by self-accusing, so here Christ means I praise thee; Ellicott renders it acknowledging with praise, Robertson prefers praise to thank, and Clarke takes it as full agreement.

Whether Christ gives thanks for the hiding is pressed carefully. Clarke insists not: he does not thank the Father for hiding these things, but that, seeing they were hidden, he revealed them to others. Robertson puts it in a phrase, that the praise is not for the ignorance of the wise but for the knowledge of the babes; Wesley reads the hiding as suffered rather than done. Chrysostom answered the question directly: Christ does not rejoice in anyone’s destruction but joys that these have known what the others have not, the revealing being joy and the concealment sorrow. The concealment, he says, is what men bring on themselves, as the apostle says God gave men over to a reprobate mind.

The wise and the babes are identified almost unanimously. Barnes takes the wise for those who thought themselves so, men of philosophy and self-conceit, and the babes for the poor and teachable; Ellicott names scribes seeking men’s praise rather than truth, against disciples who received the kingdom as a child does. Chrysostom says the wisdom is not true wisdom but what the scribes seemed to have by their talk. Gregory makes the same point: pride is condemned here, not understanding. Hilary sharpens it: babes in malice, not in understanding, the things hidden from the wise for their presumption of wisdom rather than for their wisdom. Augustine identifies the wise with the proud and asks who the babes are but the humble. Clarke supports the reversal from rabbinic sayings that when the temple fell wisdom passed from the prophets to children, and that in the Messiah’s days all wisdom would be revealed even to children.

The acquiescence at the end draws the most comment. Barnes finds in it the only satisfactory reason available, and would rest on the known will of God sooner than on his own reason, since God never errs and men constantly do. Gregory draws a lesson in humility, that we should not presume to discuss the counsels of heaven about the calling of some and the rejection of others, since what a righteous God wills cannot be unrighteous. Calvin explains whom it was for: the disciples, lest they be ashamed of a church made of the poor and despised, since we look for splendour and think nothing more incongruous than a kingdom of common people; to murmur at a decree Christ himself adores is madness rather than arrogance. Henry turns it to use: thanksgiving is the proper answer to disquieting thoughts, and praise a cordial for drooping souls. Jerome turns one phrase against those who say the Saviour was created rather than begotten: were he a creature it would be foolish to call his Maker Lord of heaven and earth and not Lord of himself too. The Gloss reads the saying as answering an unspoken doubt: why the Jews refused the Christ the Gentile world received.
26:
Gill notes that the clause is a set phrase — so is the good will before thee — often met with in Jewish forms of prayer, and takes it to designate the sovereign counsel and purpose of God, to which and to which only Christ refers the different dealings of God with men. He calls it a reason that ought to satisfy anyone and better than ten thousand others men might devise, and then rules out the alternatives: the difference cannot be owing to natural sagacity or penetration, since those belong to the very people from whom the thing is hidden; nor to any worthiness in those who receive it, since they are the poor and base and foolish of this world; nor to any foreseen better use they would make of the revelation. Robertson renders it simply as the statement that such has been the Father’s gracious will.

Ellicott translates it closely — yea, Father, that thus it was thy good pleasure — and hears the same word echoing behind two earlier scenes, the voice at the baptism declaring the Son well pleasing and the angels’ song of good will among men. He then makes a larger observation about the passage. These two verses are the only record outside the Fourth Gospel of a prayer resembling the one preserved in its seventeenth chapter, and he supposes that such prayers were usually offered apart, on the lonely hillside or in the dark, or else that the disciples shrank from recording what seemed too sacred, or beyond their capacity. This exceptional fragment stands, on his reading, as a witness that there was a whole region of the Master’s teaching the earlier reporters scarcely dared enter, and into which men were led afterwards by the disciple to whom the Spirit gave power to recall it.

Clarke calls the phrase an emphatic ratification of what precedes and fills in what was ratified: it was right that a heavenly wisdom despised and persecuted by the scribes should be offered instead to the simple, and afterwards to the Gentiles, who are wisdom’s children and justify God in his ways by bringing forth the fruit of a Gospel whose very seed the Pharisees refused.

Calvin takes the clause as a bar against enquiry. It removes every pretext for the licentiousness of questioning to which we are continually excited, since there is nothing we concede to God with more difficulty than that his will should count with us as the highest reason and justice. Scripture calls his judgments a great deep, and we plunge headlong into it to sound what is there; and if anything displeases us we gnash our teeth, or murmur, and some break out into open blasphemy. The rule Christ lays down is the opposite: whatever God has determined is to be reckoned right, and this is sober wisdom, to rest in the good pleasure of God as worth more than ten thousand arguments set before our eyes. Calvin adds the point that gives the verse its force — Christ could have produced the causes of the distinction if there were any, and instead is satisfied with the good pleasure of God and enquires no further why he calls these rather than others and composes his kingdom out of an obscure flock.
