Men turn their fury against Christ himself, he concludes, when on learning that some are freely chosen and others passed by they storm at having to let God have the last word.
27:
What all things covers is the first question. Gill restricts the delivery to Christ as mediator, since as God nothing could be delivered to one who already had every perfection of the Father, and then makes the grant as wide as possible. Jerome moves the other way, warning that conceived after our own weakness the giver would begin to go without; so the delivery may mean not heaven and earth but those who through the Son reach the Father. Ellicott takes a middle course: the words are not limited by grammar, but the context refers them to the mysteries of the kingdom implied in reveal; and he hears in them a denial of the Tempter’s claim to the power and glory of the world. Barnes reads a government of the universe committed to the Mediator for his church, and Clarke calls the sentence the key of the science of salvation.

Both press the tense. Ellicott renders it a past looking back on the moment of the gift; Robertson calls the claim sublime and refuses to let it be whittled down, since the timeless aorist points back to a moment in eternity and implies the pre-existence of the Messiah.

The older writers concentrate on the mutual knowledge. Chrysostom bars anything human from the word delivered, used so that nobody should suppose two unbegotten gods, since at his begetting he was Lord of all. That the Son alone knows the Father shows covertly that he is of one substance with him; the denial does not mean men are wholly ignorant of the Father, but that none knows him as the Son does. Nor is it said of some unknown God, and in revealing the Father the Son reveals himself. Hilary infers the same: the mutual knowledge proclaims one substance, since whoever knows the Son knows the Father in him. Augustine argues from the delivery: a Son with anything less in his power would not have all the Father has, whereas by begetting him the Father gave all that is in his own substance, which being inseparable makes it enough to name sometimes one and sometimes the other. He then notices an asymmetry others pass over: only the clause about the Father carries a promise of revelation, though this cannot mean the Son is knowable by none but the Father, since both are revealed by the Son, the light of our mind. Jerome turns the clause into a rebuke: let anyone blush who claims for himself such knowledge of Father and Son as they have of each other, since it is one thing to know by equality with God and another by his vouchsafing to reveal. Cyril of Jerusalem grades the knowledge downwards: angels behold as much as they can bear, archangels more, thrones and dominions more still, all less than his worthiness; only the Son with the Spirit knows the Father fully.

The moderns keep the doctrine in plainer terms. Barnes says no mortal can comprehend the union of divine and human in the Son, and that of a mere man this language would not have been used; Clarke divides it symmetrically, none comprehending God fully but Christ, none comprehending Christ fully but the Father. Ellicott and Robertson both note a compound verb of full knowledge and a final verb of willing. Calvin rejects the reading that makes the verse mere encouragement for preaching. Having said the Church proceeds from God’s free election, Christ now shows how that grace reaches men; for many, hearing of election, enquire anxiously how to be assured of the secret purpose and plunge into a labyrinth. Christ sends them straight to himself: life is exhibited in him and nobody shares it who does not enter by faith, so faith and predestination are joined here. Wesley states the corollary: none can know this by natural reason, but only those to whom the Son reveals it.
28:
What the coming is gets defined negatively before it is defined positively. Gill rules out a local coming, or coming to hear him preach, since his hearers had done that and many do so who never know him; and a bare submission to ordinances, since men may be baptised without having come at all. What is meant is believing on him, the going of the soul to him in desire, love, faith and hope. Remigius put it in a line: come, not with the feet but with the life, not in the body but in faith. Clarke agrees the phrase means simply believing and becoming his disciple.

Who is invited is disputed in emphasis. Barnes refers the words primarily to Jews groaning under ceremonial law and tradition, but has no doubt they are chiefly addressed to the ruined sinner trembling at his danger, and lists the rest promised: from sin, from the alarms of conscience, from the terrors of the law, from the fear of eternal death. Ellicott finds them wide enough for every form of human sin and sorrow while most prominently aimed at the burden of tradition, and notes that the first participle gives prominence to the active and the second to the passive side of suffering. Hilary makes the two classes those labouring under the Law and those burdened with the sins of the world. Clarke widens it further, applying the invitation to Jews under the Mosaic rites, to sinners wearied in iniquity, to penitents burdened with guilt and to believers oppressed by temptation; all are invited and all promised rest, and if few find it, it is because few come. Calvin narrows it sharply instead. Christ invites only those he acknowledges fit, since hypocrites intoxicated with their own righteousness would not come; and by the labouring he means not people oppressed with grief generally but those overwhelmed by their sins and alarmed at the wrath of God, whose very fainting prepares them for grace. Most despise the offer because they are not sensible of their poverty, and no venom is deadlier than the sloth bred by earthly happiness or a false opinion of one’s own virtue. Wesley divides the clauses the same way and matches a remedy to each: rest from guilt by justification and from the power of sin by sanctification.

Chrysostom hears generosity in the form of the summons: not come this man and that man, but all whoever are in trouble, sorrow or sin; not that I may exact punishment but that I may remit your sins; not that I need your glory but that I seek your salvation. The promise, he notes, is not merely salvation but something greater, being set in complete quiet. Raban says the same, that Christ will not only take the burden away but fill them with inward refreshment. Robertson calls these three verses special treasures of this Gospel alone and says no sublimer words exist; he reads the participle for burdened as a settled weariness and makes the promise causative, amounting to rejuvenation rather than rest.

Augustine traces the labour to its root, that we are mortal men carrying vessels of clay; if the vessels of flesh are straitened, he answers, the regions of love will be enlarged. The reason given is not a world made or miracles done but meekness and lowliness of heart, from which he draws his rule: whoever would be great must begin with the least, and the higher the building the deeper its foundation. He then grants an objection, that those who bend their necks to this yoke meet such hardship that they seem called not from labour to rest but from rest to labour, and answers from experience that the Spirit renews the inward man as the outward decays, since love makes hard things easy, as merchants endure storms for perishing riches and count them no hardship.
29:
The yoke is a technical term, and three commentators say so. Gill notes that the phrase is rabbinic, the Jewish doctors speaking of taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven daily and distinguishing it from the yoke of the law. Lightfoot lists the three standing phrases: the yoke of the law, the yoke of the precept, the yoke of the kingdom of heaven. Robertson adds that the rabbis used yoke for a school, as many pupils still find it one, and notes the irony that the English word school comes from the Greek for leisure while it is Jesus who offers refreshment in his. Barnes catalogues the biblical uses of the image — bondage, affliction, the punishment of sin, the commandments of God, and the ceremonies of the law — and takes it here for embracing Christ’s religion and obeying him. Ellicott makes the yoke Christ’s teaching and rule of life, explained by the words that follow, and sets it against a Pharisaic teaching too grievous to be borne. Raban makes it the Gospel that yokes Jew and Gentile in one faith, and warns that taking it up means holding it in honour rather than trampling it.

Clarke calls the command a strange paradox — a man already weary and overloaded is told to take a new weight in order to find rest — and resolves it by the psalm that bids a man cast his burden on the Lord, who will then carry both the man and his load. Barnes resolves it comparatively: all virtue implies restraint, and the question is only whose. Beside the ceremonies of the Jews, the rites of the heathen, or the laws that fashion and sensuality impose on their votaries, the requirements of Christ are mild, so it is easier to be a Christian than a sinner and religion turns out to be freedom.

The reason offered divides the readers. Ellicott puts the stress on the last two words: others might be lowly with the lowliness that is ambition’s ladder while pride reigned in their hearts, but Christ could risk seeming to boast of his humility in order to win men to prove by experience that he would hear their sorrows and turn from none with scorn. Barnes reads it as an argument rather than a self-description — the point is that this ruler is not harsh and overbearing like the Pharisees, so that obedience will be easy. Calvin rejects the common construction outright. It is a mistake, he says, to suppose Christ is assuring us of his gentleness lest his divine glory keep timid disciples at a distance; the design is rather to form us to imitate him, since the obstinacy of the flesh makes us shrink from his yoke as harsh. Only a man conformed to Christ by putting on meekness bends his neck willingly, which is why the promise of rest follows at once: when his example has accustomed us to lowliness the yoke ceases to trouble. Calvin adds a warning against abusing the earlier promise, since many turn grace into an indulgence of the flesh; the rest promised trains disciples under discipline rather than exempting them from its warfare. Clarke supplies the psychology: where pride and anger dwell there is nothing but mental labour and agony, and where the meekness of Christ dwells all is smooth and quiet. Wesley turns it into a test — whoever does not find rest of soul is not meek and lowly, and the fault lies not in the yoke but in the man who has not taken it — and glosses the taking as receiving Christ as prophet, priest and king. Ellicott notes that the promise of rest is a direct quotation from Jeremiah.
30:
The last word is the one everybody re-translates. Robertson calls easy a poor rendering and prefers kindly, noting that English has no adjective quite carrying kind and good together; the yoke of Christ is useful, good and kindly. Ellicott gives the same word a wider range — good, helpful, kind, profitable — and identifies the burden as the commandment that most characterised Christ’s teaching, that men should love one another, which those who obey find light. Wesley prefers gracious, sweet, benign and delightful, and adds that the burden, contrary to the burdens men impose, is ease, liberty and honour.

How a yoke can be light at all is the difficulty. Jerome states it in its sharpest form. The burden of sin is heavy, as the prophet witnessed who saw wickedness sitting on a talent of lead and the psalmist who found his iniquities grown too heavy for him; but how is the Gospel lighter than the Law, when the Law punished murder and adultery while the Gospel punishes anger and lust as well? His answer is that the Law commands many things the apostle says cannot be fulfilled, and requires works, whereas the Gospel seeks the will, which keeps its reward even without passing into act; the Gospel commands what lies in our power, that we do not lust. He illustrates it with a hard case: a virgin violated in a persecution is still held a virgin under the Gospel, the will being absent, while under the Law she was cast out as defiled. Raban raises the same objection from a different text, asking how the yoke can be pleasant when the way to life was called narrow, and answers that what is entered by a narrow gate is in time made broad by the unspeakable sweetness of love.

Gregory weighs the alternative. It is a cruel yoke to be subject to the things of time, to cling to what is falling, to desire what passes away and be unwilling to pass with it; for while everything flies from us against our will, what first harassed the mind with the desire of getting it now oppresses it with the fear of losing it. Against that, he asks, what burden is it to be told to shun the desires that disturb? Hilary answers by listing what the yoke requires — to abstain from wickedness, to choose good and refuse evil, to love all and hate none, to gain eternal things and not be captured by present ones, to refuse another what one would be pained to suffer — and asks what could be lighter.

Gill guards the claim. Christ calls faith in him and submission to his ordinances a yoke and a burden in allusion to the law of Moses and against the heavy loads the Pharisees laid on men’s shoulders; his commandments are not grievous but light. Yet they are not so, Gill insists, to unregenerate men, nor performable by natural strength; they are lovely in themselves and complied with cheerfully only when believers have the presence of God and the assistance of his Spirit. Clarke makes the same point positively: the Gospel imposes nothing difficult and provides for the removal of the one thing that makes men miserable, and the whole of its commandment is to love God and one’s neighbour, than which nothing could be more congenial to human nature. He also collects the rabbinic senses of the word — the yoke of the kingdom, of the law, of the precept, of repentance — and observes that it covered any binding obligation and not only the harness of oxen. Barnes closes plainly: the services required are easily rendered and not burdensome like every other system, and the Christian finds it so in peace, in joy, in comfort under evil report, in hope under persecution, and in reward for keeping the commandments.
